title: A hard drive’s head never touches the disk: it flies tens of nanometres above it

cover.alt: Inside an opened hard drive, a shiny steel arm reaches across a dark, glossy spinning platter, with a tiny head at its tip.

body: In a hard disk drive, an arm swings the read-write heads across platters spinning at thousands of revolutions per minute, writing and reading data as tiny magnetic patches. The heads don’t rest on the surface: while the disk turns, the air inside the drive holds each head up at its **flying height**, often only tens of nanometres above the platter. If a head touches the spinning surface, it can scrape away the thin magnetic coating that stores the data. That is a **head crash**, one reason drives filter the air inside them and are repaired only in dust-free rooms.

slides.alt: A close-up inside an opened hard drive: the steel arm holding the head twitches back and forth over the dark, spinning platter as the drive reads data.
slides.caption: An opened 4 GB hard drive, still running: the arm keeps nudging its head to new tracks on the spinning platter as it reads data.

slides.question: Most consumer hard drives spin at one of two speeds. What is the faster one, in revolutions per minute?
slides.explanation: Most consumer drives spin at 5,400 or 7,200 rpm. Drives range from 4,200 rpm in power-saving laptops to 15,000 rpm in high-performance servers.

slides.heading: How thin is the data layer?
slides.note: Coatings are 10–20 nm deep; IBM’s 1962 drive, the 1301, flew its heads about 6 μm up

slides.heading: Why the air matters
slides.text: The heads need air of the right density to hold them at their flying height. In thin air the heads sit lower and crash more easily, so above about 3,000 m drives must be specially sealed and pressurised. Since 2013, some drives have come sealed and filled with helium.

slides.question: What happens in a head crash?
options: The data is wiped by a magnet
slides.explanation: The head touches the spinning platter and can grind away the thin magnetic film, losing data. Shocks, power failures, dirt and wear can all cause one.
